title: Replacing the GDD with an LLM Wiki
author: daddywookie
selftext:
I’ve been spending some time building out an LLM Wiki, following the guidance created by Andrej Karpathy. It’s a really good way to bring together lots of information sources to create a knowledge base for an agent to work from. Content is ingested, turned into markdown documents by entity and topic, and then an analysis made to identify alignment and conflicts.

I’m thinking that this might be a really interesting way to create and manage a Game Design Document for use by an AI tool. In my experience, the main challenges with a GDD are keeping it up to date and consistent. The first draft is a beautifully hand crafted document and then it spirals out of control as reality hits.

What if, using the LLM wiki, you could throw in new ideas which could be automatically ingested to the right places, the agents doing the work have a single source to understand intent and then outcomes can be fed back into the wiki so it stays aligned with the actual game being built.

Has anybody here tried such a system? Can you see any immediate gotchas?

comments.author: Illustrious_Web_4208
comments.body: This is a good point could you share more. I've been asking them to update the GDD whenever we pivot but honestly I realised things change so much as we learn and grow more. I've heard about the LLM wiki but was wondering the best way to implement it?

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
I used the document shared by Karpathy and fed this into Codex and said “build this”.

https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f

I then walked through importing the first sets of sources, checking what was being created and that the agent understood its role.

Now, I just throw in content with a prompt and then periodically ask it to perform a synthesis on what it has recently learned. These synthesis pages are where the interesting insights appear as multiple sources are cross referenced. As you ask questions and receive answers you can also add these to the wiki as more knowledge to be absorbed.

This all sits on a Google drive so I can access it from other LLMs, though I am considering migrating to Git for better connectivity to iOS and Obsidian. It’s all a bit tied to my Windows desktop at the moment which doesn’t reflect my workflows.

comments.author: Triysle
comments.body:
I’ve been tinkering with doc structuring to optimize context usage with Claude Desktop. Instead of using project knowledge I use the file system extension within a specific directory of documentation.  The instructions tell the LLM where to look first (usually a small index or reference doc that describes each separate doc) and then only load the relevant references for that particular conversation.

It’s been tricky to find a good balance between cohesive memory and token bloat, and that’s with only my own contributions.  I would expect a multi-user wiki to struggle more with consistent rules for submissions.  Do you envision a huma moderating submissions like a typical wiki, or would you want the LLM to determine relevance/validity without that guidance?

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
I let the LLM decide the structure. It’s been quite good at shifting documents, changing titles and moving content around as it learns more and the focus shifts. One document might seem highly relevant until another supersedes it with a broader theme. I find it important to review the outputs of an ingest session just to keep things on track.

I’ve been pulling mainly from websites and PDFs of books. The LLM can handle the chapter structure and has built a system to track the ingest process. It also calls out strong vs weak sources, and identifies where something is a vendor pitch or a neutral guide. I suspect it would handle content from multiple different users quite nicely and act as a leveller. You could probably create instruction to call out massive deviance from the norm.

My whole wiki is around game design, development and project management. One interesting synthesis coming out is working with AI on game development and how it needs to maintain the feedback loop. AI should speed up learning, and shouldn’t increases the amount of output. I think working out how to translate the Scrum pattern of review and retro into working with an AI agent is key to this.

replies.author: Triysle
replies.body: What model are you using, if you can share?  I haven’t been able to get to that level of hands-off trust with Anthropic’s models.  Don’t get me wrong they are quite good, but the notion of handing over multi-user content curation to the LLM is still a bit much for me.  Maybe it’s a me problem more than the AI though.

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
I’m using Codex which might help keep things less creative. It has clear instructions on how to handle different media types. Also, I’m working in smaller chunks of work so I can review what it is adding to the wiki makes sense.

I think one benefit of the wiki structure as designed is that it gives things clear homes and a structure. There are topics, there are entities and there are questions and synthesis. They all link together but they are distinct records.

comments.author: AgenticGameDev
comments.body: Interesting! I use Claude.md in each modules root. And let the module facade act as the doc together with the Claude.md. But i build b2c vr experience so i don’t need character arcs and such overarching stuff

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
I don’t quite know what you mean by the module facade but I think there is an important workflow where the GDD get filled with implemented outcomes rather then ideas to be implemented. As work is completed the LLM wiki should be aware and should update itself to show where and how the idea became a reality. 

This might also help prevent duplication and provide an idea of the impact of changing direction.

I think a GDD is one great example but pretty much any product spec evolves in the same way if it is complicated enough. So many projects drown in the complexity of their own documentation until they become paralysed, or teams go rogue to chase their own goals.

comments.author: ImAvoidingABan
comments.body: You should never have to update your GDD because you shouldn’t create it until your game is ready to launch or pitch. However, I keep all my documentation and notes in Notion and just have Claude scan the entire thing once a month

comments.author: Final_Elevator_1128
comments.body: We've actually made a similar format in terminal based of Karpathy's idea of LLM Knowledge Bases. Give it a spin and let me know what you think: [https://github.com/atomicmemory/llm-wiki-compiler](https://github.com/atomicmemory/llm-wiki-compiler)

comments.author: riddlemewhat2
comments.body:
this is a really good use case

GDDs fail because they’re static, while the project evolves. an LLM wiki flips that into a living design layer that updates with the game

big wins:

* single source of truth for agents
* ideas → auto-organized into systems
* outcomes → feed back to keep it aligned

main gotcha:

* if you don’t enforce structure, it turns into messy notes again
* you need synthesis pages (systems, mechanics, decisions), not just raw ideas

this kind of approach leans into that loop:  
[https://github.com/atomicmemory/llm-wiki-compiler](https://github.com/atomicmemory/llm-wiki-compiler)

comments.author: eeigleenk
comments.body: LLM systems might work better split into acting and storing, where an agent handles decisions in real time and something like an LLM Wiki Compiler turns those into structured knowledge that persists and improves.
